recent_posts.title: Should you build your own game engine or just make a game
recent_posts.summary: A short take on whether developers should build their own game engine or use an existing one. The core argument is that building a game engine and making a game are two separate goals that rarely coexist well. Custom engine development requires mastering rendering APIs (DirectX, Vulkan), physics engines, asset pipelines, and language choices before any actual game work begins. For those who want to make games, commercially available engines like Unreal, Unity, and Godot are recommended as the practical path.

recent_posts.title: 10 playtesting lessons every indie game developer should know
recent_posts.summary: A breakdown of 10 common mistakes revealed through playtesting across 22 indie games, including: static main menus signaling an unfinished product, missing controller/keyboard tutorial parity, shipping broken demo content, omitting the game name from the main menu, ignoring known bugs, content balance issues, unfair punishing mechanics, keeping unfun mechanics out of attachment, missing tutorials, and relying on text-only tutorials. The post emphasizes that developers suffer from the 'curse of knowledge' and can never see their game with fresh eyes, making regular playtesting essential. A practical playtesting pipeline is outlined: start with friends and family, then Reddit/Discord communities, then Steam playtesting, then a public free demo, and finally Steam Next Fest.

recent_posts.title: Buy vs build in game dev depends on how much your time is worth
recent_posts.summary: A cost-benefit argument for buying game development assets versus building them from scratch. Using the Unity Asset Store summer sale as context, the author frames the buy-vs-build decision around the value of a developer's time. The example used is the author's own asset pack (36 tools for $36), arguing that unless your hourly rate is extremely low, purchasing pre-built tools is almost always more economical than building them yourself.

top_posts.title: Solo indie game developers earning millions on Steam
top_posts.summary: Solo indie game developers are achieving remarkable financial success, with recent examples like Schedule One earning $50 million and Supermarket Simulator and CCG Card Shop Simulator each earning around $30 million. This trend is attributed to increasingly powerful development tools that allow a single person to build games that previously required large teams, and Steam's uncapped revenue ceiling. While most games on Steam earn under $1,000, the potential upside is unlimited if the game resonates with players.

top_posts.title: Game dev is about illusions not simulating reality
top_posts.summary: Game development is fundamentally about creating illusions — what matters is what the player perceives, not what is technically happening under the hood. Several practical examples illustrate this principle: placing snow particles only in the player's field of view instead of the entire world, moving the world instead of the player during cutscenes, using a rotating torus to simulate an endless road, scrolling textures to fake hyperspace travel, and simple triangles to represent ocean waves in Wind Waker. The infamous Fallout 3 train (actually an NPC wearing a hat) is cited as a classic example. The core lesson is that developers should simulate only the minimum needed for the player to believe something is happening, rather than trying to replicate reality, which leads to performance problems.

top_posts.title: Incremental games are generating significant revenue on Steam
top_posts.summary: Incremental games have become a profitable genre on Steam, with recent titles generating significant revenue in short timeframes. Games like Keep on Mining ($600k in 2 weeks), Dixium ($700k in 6 months), and Cast and Chill ($1.5M total) demonstrate the commercial viability of this genre. These games focus on gradual progression through upgrades, starting simple and becoming more efficient over time, evolving from the original Cookie Clicker concept.

top_posts.title: Why indie developers should not fear sharing their game ideas
top_posts.summary: Indie developers often fear that sharing their game ideas will lead to theft, but this fear is largely unfounded. Every developer already has more ideas than they can build, and a bare idea without execution detail has little value. The only real-world scenario where copying occurs is when a game becomes massively successful — like Thronfall — and even then it's a clone of the finished product, not a stolen pitch. For most developers, obscurity is the far greater threat. The practical advice: talk about your game openly, build an audience early, and don't let secrecy sabotage discoverability.
